And the more money the bondholder’s request, the higher the bond rating will be. This rating determines how risky the bond and whether it’s a safe bet.

Now this might all sound pretty complicated, so let’s try breaking it down and see where the confusion might be coming from: 

If I invest in a bond that is rated AAA, I am essentially saying, “Sure! I’ll give you my money if you give me AAA, the highest available rating by bond rating agencies.  And if things go to plan and I don’t have to pay back this money, what happens? Well, hopefully I won’t feel so bad about taking all your money.” There might be some risk, but at the same time it’s quite low. So I’ll give you my money and if something goes wrong, the bond issuer can either pay back the money, or they can offer to buy back your bond and return the money from the issuer; it’s kind of like an insurance company buying back a risk. But in the end I’m probably saving myself a lot of money.  So if there is risk, and if there isn’t a high enough guarantee, I might not want to take it.  But I also know that the bond issuer has insurance against a lot of the risks they face, and they’re probably better off taking it.  

On the other hand, there are bonds that are rated AAA and those are probably not for you. If you invest in these, you don’t know which bond the issuer will pick, and if the bond fails to default, how the issuer will pay back the money. 

Let’s just go over an example of how an AAA-rated bond can play out: if the bond defaults (which means the issuer didn’t default). Well, if you had the chance to invest in a AAA-rated bond, the chance that you’ll get paid back is pretty high and the chance that the issuer will pay back the money is low. And if you invest in a BBB-rated bond, you risk losing half of the money you invested and getting paid back the same amount.  And that money is also at risk.  

There are more possible defaults than just AAA and BBB, so these are just an example. But you'll notice that these ratings have to do with the creditworthiness of the issuer, and how likely it is that they will default.

Now to answer your question about the investing, there are a few different things to watch out for:

The issuer’s creditworthiness.  In order to invest in bonds, you need a government, or a company that issues credit in the form of a bond.  You may think of the government as “trustworthy” because they collect taxes in an organized system, that’s why it’s hard to believe that any of them would default on their debts. But if the government defaults on its debt, how will people think about our money and government in the future? And that’s where it can be risky for investors to take on risk or exposure to these things.  
The maturity of the bond. 
How much time the bond will be in existence.  
If it’s for a very short time (such as within 3 months) you do stand to lose some money, but most people would probably take that risk.  
A company that is actually making money (not if there’s political uncertainty for example).  

There’s only so much money that people can actually invest and it might well be more than you need, which then makes it hard to find money with that level of liquidity (liquidity: how easily you can sell your bonds), especially if there is price risk.  
The next thing to watch out for is price risk. This means that if something happens, and interest rates go up and the value of the bonds decreases.  
But when it happens, investors should not look to sell immediately, instead they need to wait for whatever changes happen.  This is because money that is invested in the bond has a way to compensate for a loss, when inflation comes about an investor can take a loss on their money and increase their purchasing power with an increase in the money supply that is coming into the economy.  
This can be a good thing because with an increase in the purchasing power of money in general (more of it becomes available for spending), it becomes the investors' money that is actually making a positive impact on people and the world.  
Another thing that investors should keep in mind is that most bonds pay out at the end of a specific date, this is called a “premature” or “coupon” date.  They are mostly used because bonds are very easy to issue and invest in, so usually the prepayment is based on this date that bonds can be pre-paid.  But in times of economic uncertainty, this date can be more or less unstable.  
Another way to think about it is that any money that you’re investing in bonds needs to come back to you at the end of the same date that you funded it. This can either be the coupon date or the “maturity pay back” day, the one you actually need to know the payoff date.  
The last thing you have to watch out for is inflation risk.  If inflation happens, your purchasing power decreases and that’s bad for an investment.  
The last thing to look at are the taxes on the investment.  What taxes are involved in the bond trade that can impact the cost of capital.
